what_it_does: Training large language models on very long text sequences — millions of words at once — requires keeping enormous amounts of intermediate data in GPU memory during the forward and backward passes, quickly exceeding what any single GPU or even a cluster of GPUs holds. Existing distributed training techniques that split sequences across GPUs hit a wall because the memory spikes inside each GPU's attention computation are still enormous. FPDT (Fully Pipelined Distributed Transformer) solves this by slicing the sequence into chunks and moving each chunk's data to the CPU's much larger main memory as soon as it is done being used, while the GPU simultaneously processes the next chunk — hiding the slow transfer behind useful computation. The result: training an 8 billion-parameter model on sequences 16x longer than previously possible, using only 4 GPUs.
method_in_detail:
The problem. Training a language model on a sequence of 1 million tokens (roughly a 750,000-word document) requires storing many intermediate tensors during the computation. The attention mechanism — the core operation that lets every word look at every other word — is the worst offender: its backward pass (computing gradients to update model weights) needs 8 copies of the sequence-length-proportional data resident in GPU memory simultaneously, causing out-of-memory crashes.

Building on DeepSpeed Ulysses. FPDT extends an existing system called DeepSpeed Ulysses, which splits the sequence across multiple GPUs and uses an all-to-all shuffle (every GPU sends a slice to every other GPU) to rearrange data so each GPU handles a subset of attention heads for the full sequence. FPDT keeps this framework but adds chunked offloading.

How chunking works. The full sequence is cut into chunks (default 64,000 tokens each). The GPU processes one chunk at a time: it computes the attention output for that chunk's queries against all previously seen keys and values, then immediately moves the now-idle key/value tensors to the CPU's main memory (which is typically 1 TB, vastly larger than a GPU's 80 GB). When the next chunk needs those tensors, a prefetch operation starts transferring them back while the GPU is busy computing the current chunk — the two operations overlap in time, hiding the transfer cost.

The key design choice — double buffering. The PCIe bus connecting GPU to CPU memory is about 4x slower than the GPU's own memory bus. Chunks must be sized so that GPU computation takes at least as long as the data transfer for the next chunk; if chunks are too small the GPU starves waiting for data, too large and memory overflows. The sweet spot is 64,000 tokens. Two memory buffers alternate (double-buffering): while the GPU uses buffer A, the CPU loads the next data into buffer B, then they swap.

Sequence reordering fix. Because each GPU's chunk boundaries need to align with the attention causal mask (each token can only attend to earlier tokens), FPDT introduces a rank-ordinal scatter: data is shuffled so each GPU always processes the same contiguous slice of the overall sequence, keeping load balanced and the causal mask correct.

The result. An 8B-parameter Llama model can be trained on 2 million-token sequences using only 4 GPUs, versus the prior limit of 128,000 tokens on the same hardware. Hardware efficiency stays above 55% (meaning the GPUs spend over half their time doing useful arithmetic rather than waiting for data), compared to methods that achieve similar sequence lengths only by stacking many more GPUs.
